USA.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Close and paper a limited Phase One agreement without imposing the December 15 List 4B tariffs and without rolling back the existing 25% lists. Keep those lists, the Huawei Entity List, and the unused December 15 threat as leverage for enforcement and any later phase. Do not escalate into a Christmas consumer-goods tariff wave, and do not concede a broad proportional rollback of already-in-force tariffs until Chinese purchase, IP, currency, and enforcement text is signed and monitorable.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is moderately elevated, not existential. The United States still holds the stronger tariff instrument—List 3 at 25% since May 10, List 4A at 15% since September 1, and List 4B still scheduled for December 15—and China is at the table seeking relief (timeline 2019-05-10, 2019-09-01, 2019-10-11). That is leverage, not defeat. But the dispute is already biting U.S. interests: ISM manufacturing fell to 47.8 in September, a 10-year low, with a second month of contraction widely tied to tariffs and uncertainty; services growth slowed to a three-year weak 52.6; the IMF put the current tariff path at about -0.6% U.S. output and warned 2019 global growth is the weakest in a decade. Farm-belt exposure remains the political soft spot—China’s retaliation and earlier purchase halt hit soy and related exports, and even the October 11 “$40–50 billion” ag headline is contested (briefed sources put China’s opening offer nearer ~$20 billion and market-conditioned). Phase One as described on and after October 11 is real but thin: IP largely copyright/trademark plus already-planned investment-law language, some financial opening and currency text, Huawei explicitly outside the pact, subsidies and industrial policy deferred. Talks then slipped: APEC Chile vanished as a signing venue, a Trump–Xi ceremony was pushed toward December, MOFCOM claimed a phased tariff rollback while Navarro and outside adviser Pillsbury denied any U.S. commitment to lift existing tariffs, and China is still asking to unwind September’s 15% and even the 25% lists. The Senate’s November 19 unanimous Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act, and Beijing’s vow of countermeasures, adds a non-trade shock that could stall the commercial track. Action therefore stays near zero: negotiating without new unilateral commitments is the stance that harvests China’s desire to avoid December 15 consumer tariffs (phones, laptops, toys) while refusing to spend the 25% core lists before an enforceable text exists. Escalation now would tax U.S. households into a manufacturing slump and could collapse a deal China has already signaled it wants; a partial or full rollback now would spend leverage for an unsigned, disputed purchase number and leave structural issues for a Phase Two that may never come.
key_factors: Phase One agreed in principle Oct 11 but unsigned; Dec 15 List 4B still live
Existing 25% lists and Huawei Entity List remain the main U.S. leverage
U.S. manufacturing contraction (ISM 47.8) and farm-export exposure raise the cost of further escalation
China is demanding rollback of Sept 1 and even 25% tariffs; U.S. officials are split on whether any rollback was agreed
Purchase numbers ($40–50B vs ~$20B starting offer) and enforcement text still disputed
Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act (Senate, Nov 19) and Beijing countermeasure threats can derail the commercial track
Structural issues (subsidies, cyber, forced tech transfer, Huawei) are deferred, so core tariffs should not be spent cheaply

sources_cited.excerpt: After Washington talks, Trump announces a "Phase One" deal in principle: China to buy roughly $40–50B of US agricultural products annually; IP and currency issues also cited. Planned mid-October tariff hike delayed.
List 4A takes effect at 15% (~$110–125B of Chinese imports). China's first tranche of the ~$75B retaliation also takes effect.
US Commerce Department adds Huawei and affiliates to the Entity List. US firms generally barred from selling to Huawei without a license.
List 3 tariff rate rises from 10% to 25%.

MOFCOM said both sides agreed to cancel additional tariffs in phases; a U.S. official confirmed rollback would be part of phase one, while Peter Navarro said there is no agreement to remove existing tariffs.
China is pushing to drop the Dec. 15 tariffs on ~$156B and also the 15% Sept. 1 tariffs on ~$125B, plus relief from the earlier 25% tariffs on ~$250B.
Mnuchin said no decision yet on Dec. 15; China’s farm offer briefed near ~$20B starting vs Trump’s $40–50B; subsidies and harder structural issues left for later phases.
ISM manufacturing index fell to 47.8 in September, lowest since June 2009, second straight month of contraction, with the China dispute adding pressure.
IMF: U.S.-China tariffs drag 2019 global growth to a decade low; under the announced path U.S. output -0.6% and China -2% near term.
Senate unanimously passed the Hong Kong Human Rights and Democracy Act on Nov. 19; Beijing condemned it and vowed strong counter-measures.

CHN.rationale:
RECOMMENDATION: Stay at the table and close a narrow Phase One text now, conditioned on simultaneous, proportional cancellation of the December 15 List 4B tariffs and a first-step rollback of some existing additional duties. Offer agricultural purchases and already-teed-up market-access steps (poultry, selected farm exemptions, financial opening, IP/currency language already discussed) as the price of that tariff relief — not as a unilateral gift. Do not escalate rare-earths, the unreliable-entity list, or new detainee pressure while this window is open, and do not concede industrial-subsidy or Made-in-China-2025 structural reform in Phase One.

SUPPORTING RATIONALE: Threat is material but not existential. US tariffs already cover List 3 at 25% (raised 10 May 2019) and List 4A at 15% (~$110–125B, effective 1 Sep 2019), with List 4B (~phones, laptops, toys) still scheduled for 15 Dec unless a deal lands; that cliff hits China’s highest-value export basket. Huawei remains on the Entity List (16 May 2019; affiliates expanded Aug 2019; temporary general license only through 18 Nov), Meng Wanzhou is still held, and the 5 Aug currency-manipulator designation plus CNY through 7 added FX/political pressure. The real economy is already absorbing the war: Q2 GDP slowed to 6.2% (weakest in decades), industrial output hit a 17-year low of 5.0% in May, and US-bound goods exports are down more than 12% with firms shifting capacity to Vietnam/Indonesia. That maps above neutral and toward the +0.5 CHN anchor (export hit + Huawei targeting + FX), but not to +1.0: PMI returned above 50 in October, IP rebounded to 5.8% in September, Beijing still claims the 6–6.5% growth band, and net trade has not collapsed. Action should be mild-positive, not escalatory: Trump announced a Phase One outline on 11 Oct (ag purchases ~$40–50B, IP/currency cited, mid-October hike delayed), Liu He–Lighthizer/Mnuchin calls through mid-November were described as constructive, and MOFCOM (7 Nov) said both sides had agreed to remove additional tariffs in phases — even as Navarro and Trump publicly denied a commitment to lift existing levies and farm-purchase numbers remain a snag. Escalation now would likely lock in Dec 15 and deepen the Huawei/tech squeeze; a full concession (unconditional $50B purchases or structural SOE/subsidy giveaways) would spend leverage before Washington has matched on tariffs. Negotiate — lock the easy phase, insist rollback scale matches the agreement, keep Huawei/Meng and core industrial policy off this text.
key_factors: Dec 15 List 4B cliff still live on phones/laptops/toys
Existing 25% List 3 and 15% List 4A already taxing the export machine
Huawei Entity List + Meng detention remain outside the Phase One text
Growth/IP/export-hub stress is real but not a financial-stability break
Phase One is advanced enough to trade farm purchases for tariff standstill/rollback
White House is divided on rolling back existing tariffs — do not pre-concede
